passages.text: At dawn Peter came in and said, “Let Clement, his mother Mattidia, and my wife sit together in the carriage.” And so it was done. As we set out on the road toward Balaneae, my mother asked me how my father was doing. I said, “He went away in search of you and my twin brothers, Faustinus and Faustinianus, and cannot be found. I think he has died, given how long it has been, either suffering shipwreck, meeting disaster on the road, or wasting away with grief.” When she heard this, she became tearful and sighed in sorrow. Yet her joy at finding me somewhat softened the grief the recollection brought. We arrived at Balaneae. On the following day we came to Paltus, and from there to Gabala; on the next we arrived at Laodicea. There, before the gates, Nicetas and Aquila met us, kissed us warmly and led us to our lodging. Seeing that it was a fine, large city, Peter said, “It is worthwhile to stay here for some days, for generally a large population is better able to produce the people being sought.” Nicetas and Aquila asked me who this unfamiliar woman was. I said, “My mother, whom God granted me to recognize through my master Peter.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: given how long it has been
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase is read temporally, with a long interval understood from the father’s unresolved absence: that elapsed time grounds Clement’s inference of death. “Most likely” is a possible probability-oriented rendering, but it does not directly preserve the contextual basis in elapsed time; the revised main text therefore prefers the temporal interpretation. Death remains an inference expressed by “I think,” not verified knowledge.
Peter’s generalization about a crowd can refer to missing persons in this recognition narrative; it can also mean the people sought for his mission. The main text does not specify which group.
κύριος here is a respectful human title for Peter, not an identification with the divine Lord. “My lord Peter” is the more formal alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ καταφιλήσαντες ἦγον ἐπὶ τὴν ξενίαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: kissed us warmly and led us to our lodging
lexical_decisions.rationale: καταφιλήσαντες expresses affectionate kissing; no separate embrace is added. The source elsewhere distinctly names embraces when it intends them.

passages.text: When she had had enough sleep and awakened, Peter began speaking with my mother about reverence for God, saying first, “Woman, I want you to know the way of life of our religion. We worship one God, who made the world you see, and we keep his law. Its first requirements include worshiping him alone, treating his name as holy, honoring parents, being chaste, and living pleasantly. In addition, since we do not live without distinctions, we do not partake of the nations’ table; indeed, we cannot even dine with them, because they live impurely. But whenever we persuade them to think and do what belongs to the truth, and baptize them with a certain thrice-blessed invocation, then we gather at table with them. Even if someone happens to be a father, mother, wife, child, brother, or anyone else who feels natural affection, we cannot dare to dine with that person: we do this as a distinctive religious practice. So do not regard your son’s not dining with you as an insult, until you think and do the same things as he does.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied adjective’s adverbial form refers to pleasant living; it is not changed to a conjectural “uprightly” or made a command to indulgence.
The singular description of a naming or invocation is retained; no specific baptismal formula or persons are supplied.

lexical_decisions.chosen: we do this as a distinctive religious practice
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression can also be understood as “we do this especially on religious grounds.” The main wording keeps the religious distinction and does not present the rule as a universal modern obligation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἢ ἄλλος τις ἐκ φύσεως στοργὴν ἔχων
lexical_decisions.chosen: or anyone else who feels natural affection
lexical_decisions.rationale: The active participle ἔχων makes that other person the holder of affection. Its object is unexpressed and is not replaced by a different, unnamed person who feels affection toward this one.

passages.text: While my mother was saying this, the boys, who were listening as Peter had advised, could no longer contain themselves. They stood up and embraced her, weeping abundantly and covering her with kisses. She said, “What does this mean?” Peter answered, “Woman, steady your mind courageously, so that you may enjoy your children. These are your sons Faustinus and Faustinianus, whom you said had died in the depths. How they are alive, after dying in your presence on that extremely dreadful night, and how one of them is now called Nicetas and the other Aquila, they themselves will be able to tell you. We too have to learn it along with you.” When Peter said this, my mother was so overjoyed that she nearly died from faintness. When we revived her, she sat down, came to herself, and said, “My longed-for children, please tell us what happened to you after that terrible night.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: Peter echoes her belief about the shipwreck rather than independently asserting an actual death and resurrection. “Having died as far as you were concerned” is a contextual alternative; the main text keeps the sharper surviving wording.

χαλεπωτάτῃ is superlative and may have elative force, “extremely dreadful.” This preserves its intensification while not requiring a uniquely worst night. “Most dreadful” is the formal superlative alternative; the later positive χαλεπή remains “terrible.”

passages.text: Nicetas, henceforth Faustinus, began to speak: “That very night, when the ship was breaking apart, as you know, some men who were not afraid to plunder in the depths picked us up and put us in a boat. Rowing, they took us sometimes along the shore and sometimes sent for provisions, bringing us to Strato’s Caesarea. There, with us weeping from hunger, fear, and blows—all to keep us from rashly saying anything they did not want said—and after also changing our names, they managed to sell us. A very distinguished woman named Justa, a convert to the Jews, bought us, kept us in the place of children, and diligently educated us in every branch of Greek learning. As we grew up and became sensible, we loved the religion and applied ourselves to learning, so that in discussions with the other nations we could expose their error. We also mastered the philosophers’ teachings, especially the most godless—I mean those of Epicurus and Pyrrho—so that we could refute them more effectively.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: kept us in the place of children
lexical_decisions.rationale: Their purchase and subsequent treatment are both retained. The text does not explicitly describe a legal adoption or manumission.
The superlative belongs to the narrator’s evaluation of the philosophers, not an added evaluation by the translator.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κἀκεῖ δακρύοντας ἡμᾶς λιμῷ φόβῳ τε καὶ πληγαῖς, ὅπως μή τι προπετὲς λαλήσωμεν τῶν αὐτοῖς μὴ δοκούντων, ἔτι δὲ καὶ τὰ ὀνόματα ἡμῶν ἀλλάξαντες, πωλῆσαι ἠδυνήθησαν.
lexical_decisions.chosen: with us weeping from hunger, fear, and blows—all to keep us from rashly saying anything they did not want said—and after also changing our names, they managed to sell us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative hunger, fear, and blows accounts for the children’s weeping and coercive treatment, rather than directly describing the means of a sale. The ὅπως-clause gives the purpose of that coercion; the subsequent renaming is introduced as an additional act. The revision keeps those attachments instead of assigning the speech-prevention purpose exclusively to renaming.

passages.text: “Having become almost companions from childhood with a certain magician, Simon, we came close to being deceived through friendship. There is an account about a certain man: when he appears in kingship, the [ὁ ... ων] of those who have revered God will be able to live immortally and without pain. But these things, mother, will be explained to you more precisely at the proper time. Just when we were about to be deceived by Simon, a companion of our master Peter, called Zacchaeus, took us in and warned us not to be deceived by the magician. When Peter arrived, he brought us to him, so that, by giving us full assurance, he might persuade us about the matters pertaining to reverence for God. Therefore, mother, we also pray that you may share in the good things we have been granted, so that we may partake of salt and table together. This, then, mother, is why you thought we had died: on that dreadful night pirates carried us off on the open sea, while you supposed we had perished.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase may indicate appearing in royal rule or within a kingdom; the main text chooses the former without supplying a realm or identifying the man.
The concrete shared-meal language is retained rather than reduced to social friendship.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὗ φανέντος ἐν βασιλείᾳ τῶν θεοσεβησάντων ὁ ... ων ἀθανάτως καὶ ἀλύπως βιῶσαι ἔχει
lexical_decisions.chosen: when he appears in kingship, the [ὁ ... ων] of those who have revered God will be able to live immortally and without pain
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text attaches τῶν θεοσεβησάντων, “of those who have revered God,” to the incomplete subject marked by ὁ ... ων. This is supported by the contrast between the appearing man and the group benefiting from immortal, painless life, but it does not restore that subject’s missing letters. A material alternative attaches the genitive to βασιλείᾳ: “when he appears in the kingdom/kingship of those who have revered God, the [ὁ ... ων] will be able to live immortally and without pain.” Neither attachment is uniquely established; the three-dot gap remains unchanged and no lost wording is supplied.

source_issues.issue: The edition prints a three-dot gap with surviving ὁ and ων around it. These are retained literally as [ὁ ... ων], without restoring a person, group, or participle. The surrounding phrase is therefore visibly incomplete; the missing content has not been recovered.
